chunks: Luqman said to his son: 'O my son! Choose the gatherings according to your own discernment. If you see a group mentioning Allah, Majestic and Mighty, then sit with them. If you happen to be knowledgeable, your knowledge will benefit you, and if you happen to be ignorant, they will teach you, and perhaps Allah will shade them with His mercy and cover you along with them.

And when you see a group who are not mentioning Allah, do not sit with them. If you happen to be knowledgeable, your knowledge will not benefit you, and if you happen to be ignorant, they will increase you in ignorance, and perhaps Allah will inflict them with His punishment and cover you along with them.'

key_terms.الْمَجَالِسَ: Gatherings, assemblies, scholarly circles (majalis) — the social-spiritual environment one inhabits
key_terms.جَلَّ وَعَزَّ: Majestic and Mighty — a standard paired divine epithet emphasizing transcendence and power
key_terms.رَحْمَةٌ: Mercy — divine grace that descends upon righteous gatherings, protecting all who participate
key_terms.عَلَى عَيْنِكَ: Literally 'with your own eye' — meaning with careful personal discernment, not casually
key_terms.عُقُوبَةٌ: Punishment/retribution — divine chastisement that falls on heedless gatherings and endangers bystanders
key_terms.يَذْكُرُونَ اللَّهَ: Those who remember/mention Allah — dhikr as the defining criterion of righteous company

ai.seo_question: What did Luqman advise his son about choosing companions and gatherings in Islam?
ai.summary: This narration transmits the wisdom of Luqman, a figure mentioned in the Quran (Surah Luqman 31) as a recipient of divine wisdom, advising his son on the critical importance of choosing one's companions and gatherings wisely. The teaching establishes a dual principle: those who remember God elevate all who sit with them — the learned benefit from their knowledge, the ignorant receive instruction — while those heedless of God corrupt everyone around them. Al-Kulayni's scholars in the 3rd–4th century AH would have understood this as practical guidance for navigating scholarly networks in which circles of hadith transmission were inseparable from spiritual formation.
